newsitem.title: USA: House Democrat vows to strike tobacco tax break.
newsitem.headline: House Democrat vows to strike tobacco tax break.

text.p: House Minority Leader Richard Gephardt said on Tuesday he will seek to repeal a tax break given to the tobacco industry in a tax-cut bill President Clinton just signed into law.

In a letter to Clinton, the Missouri Democrat said the tobacco break was unknown to lawmakers before they cast their vote last week for balanced budget spending and tax bills. Gephardt voted for neither.
"The American taxpayer deserves better than this special interest giveaway that sidesteps public accountability through back-room deals and under-the-table favours," Gephardt wrote.

The president signed into law a cigarette tax increase -- 10 cents a pack in 2000 and another five cents in 2002 -- as part of a balanced budget spending bill. In a separate $95 billion tax-cut bill he also signed, the tobacco industry won a valuable break which allows a write-off of the cigarette tax hike against their liability under the proposed national tobacco settlement. The tax is currently 24 cents a pack.
Clinton has until Monday to decide whether to allow some 79 special tax provisisions to take effect even though he has already signed the tax bill.

However, the president's as-yet untested power to veto provisions that benefit only a handful of companies or individuals may not apply to the tax break given to the tobacco industry. If it does not apply, or is not used, Gephardt said he will introduce legislation to repeal the tobacco break.
Other lawmakers said they will seek to recoup the lost tax by raising the eventual price tag on the tobacco settlement.
Several Democratic lawmakers urged the president to strike many other provisions in the tax cut bill.

Representative Tom Barrett of Wisconsin cited as veto-bait tax breaks for hard cider producers, for computer software exporters and for U.S. shareholders in foreign insurance, banking and securities corporations.

If Clinton exercises the line-item veto, Congress would have 30 days when it comes back into session in September to reverse his decisions. A reinstatement of the tax breaks would require a two-thirds vote in favour of doing so.
